backups.name: Southwest Route / Standard
backups.fa: Lorenz A. Nelson and a Mountaineers party, 1921 (first ascent of the peak)
gear: map, compass, GPS (route-finding near the col)
water filter/treatment (seasonal sources at high camp)
hazards: loose rock/talus on the west ridge and upper mountain
early-season snow and cornices near the Fortress-Chiwawa col
misidentifying the correct gully near the col — the wrong line leads to an exposed low-5th-class dead end
long remote approach with no reliable cell coverage
rough, high-clearance-only Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) access
backups.overview: Chiwawa Mountain (8,459') is a remote summit in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. Its parent peak, Fortress Mountain (8,760'), lies about 1.1 miles west across the Fortress-Chiwawa col, and the two are commonly combined from a shared high camp. A small remnant of the Lyman Glacier clings to Chiwawa's northeast slope above Lyman Lake, but that is a separate, more involved approach on the far side of the mountain; the standard southwest route described here is a non-glaciated, largely cross-country scramble (Class 2-3) up scree, heather, and early-season snow to the west ridge, finishing on cairned Class 2 terrain to the summit. First climbed in 1921 by a Mountaineers party led by Lorenz A. Nelson.
backups.beta: Ascend the southwest snowfield and scree slopes to reach the summit at 8,459 feet. The route follows the path of least resistance from Fortress-Chiwawa Col, traversing east-northeast aiming for the col, then ascending the final south ridge. Navigate snow or scree to within 100 feet of the summit, then traverse the west side to avoid steep rock sections on the final approach.
backups.turnaround: The turnaround point from camp should be mid-afternoon to ensure safe descent in daylight. In early summer with longer daylight hours, routes should still descend before darkness, with particular attention to safe river crossing and trail navigation.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage on the approach or summit area; carry a satellite messenger/PLB.
backups.descent: Down-climb the cairned west ridge back to the Fortress-Chiwawa col basin, then descend scree/snow to high camp; no rappels needed on the standard line.

waypoints.name: Trinity Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Chiwawa River Road FR 6200; self-issue wilderness permit and a Northwest Forest Pass or $5/day recreation pass required at the kiosk; vault toilet, no potable water.
waypoints.directions: Drive Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) to its end at the old Trinity mine site. The road is rough and high clearance is worth having; it commonly stays snowbound until early summer, which sets the start of the season here more than conditions on the peak do. Carry water from home — there is none at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Buck Creek Trail / Chiwawa River Trail fork
waypoints.note: Bear right off Buck Creek Trail #1513 onto Chiwawa River Trail #1550, which follows an old mining-road grade up the valley.
waypoints.directions: Start up-valley on Buck Creek Trail #1513 for about a mile and a half. Bear right at the fork; #1550 takes over an old mining-road grade and stays close to the river, so water is reliable along this whole stretch.

waypoints.name: Red Mountain Trail junction
waypoints.note: Stay on Chiwawa River Trail #1550 toward Chiwawa Basin; the other fork climbs to Red Mountain and Buck Creek Pass instead.
waypoints.directions: A couple more easy miles on the old road bed beside the river. This is the last water that is both obvious and easy to reach before the basin, so fill here — the tread beyond the junction gets rougher and braids in places.

waypoints.name: Chiwawa River ford
waypoints.note: Cold, knee-deep ford of the Chiwawa River (crossed once in, once out); tread gets brushy and faint beyond this point.
waypoints.directions: Past the junction the trail deteriorates and climbs through forest toward the basin. The crossing is unbridged and there is no way around it; it is manageable at typical summer flow but higher and pushier early in the season, so take the time to pick a line rather than accepting the first one. Note the spot, since you cross it again on the way out.

waypoints.name: Leave trail in upper Chiwawa Basin
waypoints.note: Maintained tread peters out in the basin's upper meadows; begin cross-country travel toward the 6,300 ft camp benches, following sporadic flagging.
waypoints.directions: Above the ford the brush thickens and the tread fades and braids. Favour the more open, less-timbered ground along the east side of the basin — drifting into the timber turns this into a bushwhack. Watch for a faint branch near the meadow edge that is easy to walk straight past; if you miss it, aim for the obvious basin above and pick your way up through the generally open forest.

waypoints.name: Chiwawa Basin high camp benches
waypoints.note: Small dirt benches with just enough flat ground for two tents; water from small trickling streams nearby; the standard overnight base for the col.
waypoints.directions: Several lines reach the bench from the basin. The left-trending gully is the most direct and the easiest going, though it is wet; the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the alternative and are the better choice coming down. Early season these are snow gullies, faster than the loose summer scree but worth an ice axe.

waypoints.name: Fortress-Chiwawa col (notch on Fortress's east ridge)
waypoints.note: Moderate snow slope steepens noticeably near the notch (ice axe recommended); rock off to the sides is loose and sandy.
waypoints.directions: From the bench traverse steep heather and aim for the notch in Fortress's east ridge. The snow slope leading up to it is moderate but steepens noticeably in the last stretch below the notch, and the rock flanking it is loose and sandy — stay on the snow or the most solid line you can find rather than escaping onto the sides.

waypoints.name: Chiwawa Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Two summit rocks about 30 ft apart with little to distinguish which is the true high point; views of Glacier Peak and Fortress Mountain.
waypoints.directions: From the col work up the southwest side on slabs, gullies and talus, taking the path of least resistance rather than any single line. The crux is the short step gaining the summit ridge — loose, exposed Class 2-3 — after which an easy traverse of about 100 ft to the west/right reaches the top. Picking the wrong gully near the col is the standard mistake here and leads to an exposed low-fifth-class dead end, so back off and re-read the terrain rather than forcing it.

From camp, cross crusty morning snow slopes up to the broad saddle near 8,200 ft between Chiwawa and Fortress, then work up the southwest snowfield/talus with a short Class 2-3 led…
sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Summit day: Chiwawa Mountain via SW snowfield

sectionBreakdown.note: Retrace the Red Mountain mining road/Chiwawa River Trail back down through the brushy lower miles to the trailhead.

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed on the standard Class 2-3 line; bring an ice axe (light traction optional) for firm snow on the approach and near the col into early-mid summer. A rope/small rack only comes into play if combining with Fortress Mountain's Class 3-4 east ridge, or if you stray off the cairned line into the low-5th-class gully some parties have mistakenly followed.
pro_tips: Commonly combined with Fortress Mountain (8,760', Class 3-4 east ridge) from the same high camp near the Fortress-Chiwawa col — this is a different basecamp than Lyman Lake/Spider Gap, which serves the separate, glaciated NE side of Chiwawa
Cairns mark the normal Class 2 line on the west ridge; parties report a nearby gully that dead-ends in low-5th-class rock — don't follow it
High camp is typically on benches around 6,300' with small, seasonal water sources
The final 10-12 miles of Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) to Trinity Trailhead is rough gravel/dirt — a high-clearance vehicle is recommended
watch_out: loose rock/talus on the upper mountain and west ridge
misidentifying the col gully — the wrong line leads to an exposed low-5th-class dead end
early-season snow and cornices near the col
long rough access road limiting vehicle options
this is not the glaciated Lyman Glacier route — no crevasse hazard on the standard SW line, but also no glacier descent shortcut
backups.pro_needs: Non-technical Class 2-3 scramble on the standard line; an ice axe covers firm snow on the approach and col through early-mid summer. No rope, rack, or crevasse-rescue gear is needed on this side of the mountain unless you detour onto the glaciated NE (Lyman Glacier) side or add Fortress Mountain's Class 3-4 east ridge.
backups.best_season: Late June through September is the reliable window. The Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) to Trinity Trailhead typically isn't fully open/melted out until around mid-June, and the upper mountain and col can hold snow into July in heavy-snow years.
backups.approach: Park at Trinity Trailhead (~2,800 ft), at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old Trinity mine site. From the trailhead, hike the Buck Creek Trail #1513 up the valley; at roughly 1.4–1.5 miles, bear right (northeast) at the junction onto the Chiwawa River Trail #1550, an old mining-road grade that continues up-valley along the river (reliable water the whole way here). Follow the Chiwawa River Trail about 3.7 more miles to the signed Red Mountain Trail junction at Chiwawa Mountain's southeastern foot — roughly 5 miles and the last easy, obvious water before the basin. Most parties bear left here into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain. The tread beyond the junction is rougher and sometimes braided; it climbs about a mile-plus through forest and then subalpine meadow toward the ~5,500 ft basin below the Fortress-Chiwawa col. Expect a shallow ford of the Chiwawa River/headwater creek in this stretch, and favor the more open, less-timbered ground along the east side of the basin to avoid brush-whacking. Above the basin, gain the ~6,300 ft bench via talus/scree gullies or vegetated slopes just left of them — early-season parties will find snow gullies here (ice axe/crampons recommended) that are faster than the loose summer scree. From the bench, the standard finish is a class 2 scramble up slabs and gullies on the southwest face; the short section gaining the summit ridge is the route's crux — loose, exposed class 2–3 rock — after which an easy ~100 ft rightward (west) traverse leads to the summit. One-way distance from Trinity is roughly 7–8 miles with about 5,700 ft of gain; most parties camp in Chiwawa Basin or on the 6,300 ft bench and treat it as an overnight, though fit parties do it car-to-car in a long day. A less-traveled alternate approach starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead, bushwhacking to about 5,500 ft and following a gully right of Point 5971 up to the col west of the summit, then easy Class 2 along the west ridge.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the southwest scree/gully slopes to the 6,300 ft bench, staying off the looser climber's-left skyline gully in favor of the main descent gullies/vegetated slopes used on the way up. Continue down into Chiwawa Basin, re-ford the creek, and retrace the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 and Buck Creek Trail #1513 back to the Trinity Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling anywhere on it — none is typically required. Watch for loose rock and scree underfoot on the upper southwest slopes (a common complaint on nearby Fortress Mountain's gullies applies here too), and in early season the same gullies used for the ascent can be glissaded or skied for a much faster descent when snow-covered.
backups.bail: The standard line is reversible almost anywhere without rappelling — retreat down the cairned west ridge and scree slopes to camp. The main retreat hazard is losing the cairned line in the gully system near the col; if the terrain steepens into low-5th-class rock, back off and find the easier line.

pitch_detail.notes: From Fortress-Chiwawa Col, the terrain is moderate. Bushwhacking section from river to col can be steep and brushy. Establish camp at 6,300-foot bench.

Ascend snow and rock traverse northeast from col toward summit ridge. Route finding can be tricky in poor visibility. Snow provides good climbing conditions early season; transitions to scree by late summer.

Climb southeast along ridge, then traverse west side to avoid steep rock on final 100 feet. Shattered rock with loose sections; careful footwork required. Traverse around west side to reach summit block.

itinerary.cal: Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) typically isn't fully snow-free/passable until mid-June, and the route holds snow into summer, so most ascents happen late June through September.

days.note: From the Chiwawa River / Trinity trailhead (2,800 ft), follow Chiwawa River Trail #1550 along the old Red Mountain mining road, passing the Buck Creek and Chiwawa Basin trail junctions around 4,800 ft. The lower trail is brushy/overgrown in summer; expect a long, steady climb through forest into open basin terrain for camp.
days.title: Approach to high camp
days.objective: Reach high camp near 5,900-6,300 ft on the old Red Mountain mining road

days.note: From camp, cross crusty morning snow slopes up to the broad saddle near 8,200 ft between Chiwawa and Fortress, then work up the southwest snowfield/talus with a short Class 2-3 ledge traverse to the summit ridge. Many parties tag Fortress Mountain's Class 3-4 east ridge from the same col on the same day.

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-3 day trip for most parties: ~19-20 miles round trip with roughly 5,700 ft cumulative gain/loss; camp sits near 5,900-6,300 ft on the old mining road, with a long (7+ hr) summit push on day two. Very strong parties have done it car-to-car in a single ~14-16 hr day.

access.fees: $5 per vehicle per day, or $30 for an annual pass, at Trinity Trailhead.
access.rules: Glacier Peak Wilderness rule: no wood campfires above 3,500 ft elevation — this covers essentially the entire route and approach, so stoves only. Camping is also restricted within 200 ft of Lyman Lake/Holden Lake shorelines and 1/4 mile of Image Lake if approaching via those basins. Free self-issue wilderness permit required at the trailhead.
access.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or reservation system for this area.
access.closures: Forest Road 6200 is closed under Forest Service order 06-17-07-2026-11 from the Atkinson Flats Campground junction north to Trinity — Trinity Trailhead is NOT accessible by vehicle. The closure took effect May 20, 2026 (damage from a December 2025 storm/rain event: washouts, slides, plugged culverts) and runs through December 31, 2027 unless rescinded sooner, with no reopening estimate given. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes FR 6200 and the Chiwawa River Trail. Check current Wenatchee River Ranger District alerts before planning a trip.
access.landManager: Wenatchee River Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Glacier Peak Wilderness); (509) 548-2550
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at some trailheads (fee day-use sites) — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass, Digital Day Pass, or Interagency Recreation Pass accepted at Trinity Trailhead

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk (Phelps Creek, Trinity, Entiat River, or the Holden trailheads). Holden Village and its access road are closed to hikers through at least summer 2026.

road.name: Chiwawa River Road / Forest Road 6200
road.status: paved for roughly the first 8-11 miles from Chiwawa Loop Road, then rough gravel/dirt for the final ~10-12 miles to Trinity Trailhead
road.driveNote: From Coles Corner on US-2, take WA-207 north 4.4 miles, then Chiwawa Loop Road and FR 6200 about 23 miles total to Trinity Trailhead (2,800'); the final stretch is not recommended for low-clearance vehicles.
road.seasonalGate: Usually not fully accessible until the road melts out/is cleared, often mid-to-late June. The road is additionally closed from Atkinson Flats Campground north to Trinity under Forest Service order 06-17-07-2026-11 (effective May 20, 2026 through Dec 31, 2027), due to December 2025 storm damage — Trinity Trailhead is NOT reachable by vehicle. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes the road and the Chiwawa River Trail. Check Wenatchee River Ranger District alerts before driving.

climate.typical: East-slope North Cascades climate: drier and sunnier than the west-side crest, but the elevation still holds a substantial snowpack into summer; afternoon thunderstorms are common in July-August.

bySeason.fall: Good stable weather often persists into September/early October, then increasing chance of new snow at elevation.
bySeason.spring: Full snow cover on the approach and upper mountain; avalanche hazard on slopes near the col; Chiwawa River Road usually still gated or snowed in.
bySeason.summer: Prime season; snow retreats from the trail and lower slopes by July, though the col and upper ridge can hold snow into July in heavy years.
bySeason.winter: Road closed/snowed in; full winter mountaineering conditions, essentially inaccessible.

climate.forecastZone: No NWAC zone covers this drainage specifically; the nearest official avalanche guidance is NWAC's Stevens Pass (east-side) zone — treat it as approximate for the Chiwawa/Buck Creek Pass area.

emergency.notes: Chiwawa Mountain sits on the Chelan/Snohomish county line within the Glacier Peak Wilderness, but the standard SW-route trailheads (Trinity, Phelps Creek) are reached from the Chelan County side via the Chiwawa River drainage. Cell coverage is unreliable to absent for the entire approach and climb — carry a satellite messenger/PLB.
emergency.rangerStation: Wenatchee River Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — (509) 548-2550
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center, 817 Commercial St, Leavenworth, WA — 24-hour Emergency Department; the closest hospital to the Chiwawa River Road trailheads.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 for emergencies; Chelan County Sheriff non-emergency (509) 667-6851, dispatched via RiverCom 911

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends in late July and August when the approach trail is snow-free
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low - likely a small handful of roped parties per season; the Spider Meadows/Lyman Lakes approach trail is a popular backpacking destination, but very few of those hikers continue onto the glacier and summit route

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strenuous multi-day approach (Trinity Trailhead up the Chiwawa River Trail to a high camp on the ~6,300 ft benches) with significant elevation gain before the climb even begins
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight camping kit plus ice axe (and light traction early season); no rope, harness or crevasse-rescue gear on the standard line; roughly 35-40 lb

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - typically a full day to reach a high camp on the benches above Chiwawa Basin before a summit push
requiredSkills: Ice axe self-arrest and crampon technique
Class 3-4 scrambling on loose/rotten alpine rock
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate to advanced - solid off-trail scrambling experience; comfort on exposed Class 3-4 rock while tired from a long approach

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through early September, once the approach is largely melted out and before early fall storms

July.reason: The approach is usually open, though snow often lingers in the gullies and near the col, especially early in the month

June.reason: Access road/trail may still be snowed in or gated, and lingering deep snowpack makes travel and route-finding harder

August.reason: Best combination of stable weather and a mostly snow-free approach

September.reason: Days shorten and early fall storms can return

weather.typical: Central Cascades alpine climate with heavy winter snowpack that lingers in the upper basin; the best summer window is stable but short
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms/convective buildup are a common summer hazard in this part of the North Cascades, especially July-August

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Exposed Class 3-4 scrambling on loose, rotten rock on the summit ridge; combined with the long, committing, remote approach, any fall or injury here carries serious consequences given the distance from help

avalanche.zone: No NWAC zone specifically covers this peak, and NWAC's daily forecasts are only issued for the winter season (roughly Nov-Apr), which does not overlap the Jul-Sep climbing window for this route

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - the standard southwest route is non-glaciated and does not cross the Lyman Glacier remnant, which lies on a separate, more involved approach on the mountain's northeast side (see overview)

gaps: Round-trip mileage varies significantly by source depending on whether Fortress Mountain is combined into the same trip (roughly 14-16 mi for Chiwawa alone vs. ~20 mi in combined Chiwawa+Fortress trip reports) — no single dist_km value was reliable enough to record
No verified GPS coordinates for the high camp or Fortress-Chiwawa col beyond the summit waypoint already on file
NWAC does not publish a forecast zone specific to this drainage, so avalanche-forecast applicability is approximate

approach_logistics.trailhead: Trinity Trailhead (end of Chiwawa River Road)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Park at Trinity Trailhead (~2,800 ft), at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old Trinity mine site.

approach_variants.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to Chiwawa Basin and the 6,300 ft benches
approach_variants.notes:
Park at Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old mine site. Start up-valley on Buck Creek Trail #1513 for about a mile and a half and BEAR RIGHT at the fork onto Chiwawa River Trail #1550, which takes over an old mining-road grade close to the river — water is reliable along all of this.

About 3.7 more miles brings the signed Red Mountain Trail junction near 4,000 ft. This is the last water that is both obvious and easy to reach before the basin, so fill here. Bear LEFT into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain.

Beyond the junction the tread deteriorates, braids and climbs through forest toward the basin, with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater around 4,400 ft — manageable at summer flow, higher and pushier early. Above the ford the brush thickens and the tread fades: favour the more open, less-timbered ground along the EAST side of the basin, because drifting into the timber turns this into a bushwhack.

Camp is on benches around 6,300 ft. Several lines reach them: the left-trending gully is the most direct and easiest going though it is wet, and the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better choice coming down.

FR-6200 has been closed to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat since May 20, 2026 under storm-damage order 06-17-07-2026-11 (through December 31, 2027), so Trinity is not reachable by vehicle. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40) also closes the Chiwawa River Road and the trails from Trinity through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Sep. The road to Trinity is often not melted out until mid-June, and the upper mountain and col hold snow into July in heavy years
hazards: Misidentifying the gully near the col, which leads to an exposed low-fifth-class dead end
Loose, sandy rock flanking the col and loose talus on the upper mountain
Cornices and early-season snow at the Fortress-Chiwawa col
An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater, and fading braided tread that becomes a bushwhack if you drift into timber
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat since May 20, 2026 (order 06-17-07-2026-11, through December 31, 2027), so Trinity is unreachable by vehicle
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A NOTCH IN SOMEBODY ELSE'S RIDGE, AND SAYING IT THAT WAY IS WHAT MAKES IT FINDABLE: the Fortress-Chiwawa col at about 7,200 ft is the NOTCH IN FORTRESS MOUNTAIN'S EAST RIDGE. From the 6,300 ft benches, traverse steep heather and aim for that notch. You are walking toward a gap on the skyline of the mountain NEXT DOOR, not toward the peak you are climbing.

WHAT THE LAST STRETCH FEELS LIKE, so you know you are on it: the snow slope up to the col is moderate and then steepens noticeably in the final section below the notch, and the rock flanking it is loose and sandy. Stay on the snow or on the most solid line you can find rather than the flanking rock. A slope that stays uniformly moderate all the way to a gap is not this one.

FROM THE COL THE ROUTE HAS NO SINGLE LINE AND THAT IS THE CORRECT ANSWER, NOT A GAP IN THE BETA: work up the south-west side on slabs, gullies and talus taking the path of least resistance. Nothing here is cairned or named.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS EXPLICIT AND IT HAS A STATED CONSEQUENCE: misidentifying the correct gully near the col leads to an exposed low-fifth-class DEAD END. If the ground you are on has stopped offering an easy option and is committing you to fifth-class moves, reverse and pick a different line — this route never needs them.

THE CRUX IS SHORT AND IT IS AT THE TOP: the step gaining the SUMMIT RIDGE is loose and exposed Class 2-3 and is the hardest ground on the route. After it, an easy traverse of about 100 ft to the WEST — to your right — reaches the top. If you gain a ridge and the summit is to your left, you are on the wrong section of crest.

GOING BACK DOWN, USE A DIFFERENT LINE THAN YOU CAME UP FOR ONE STRETCH ONLY: below the benches, the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better descent, and the loose climber's-left skyline gully should be avoided.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek variant to the col west of the summit
approach_variants.notes:
A less-travelled alternative starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead rather than Trinity. It bushwhacks to about 5,500 ft and follows a gully to the right of Point 5971 up to the col WEST of the summit, then takes easy Class 2 ground along the west ridge to the top.

This is the shorter line on paper and the rougher one on the ground: there is no tread on the bushwhack and no camp equivalent to the Chiwawa Basin benches. It is genuinely used, but not recommended over the Trinity approach.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Sep, as for the main line
hazards: An unmaintained bushwhack with no tread from about 5,500 ft and no published landmarks below the gully
No established camp on this side, so it commits you to a long day
Early-season snow in the gully and at the col
Loose rock on the west ridge, as everywhere on this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS VARIANT'S BASE IS A DIFFERENT COL FROM THE MAIN ROUTE'S, AND CONFUSING THE TWO PUTS YOU ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN. The standard line goes to the FORTRESS-CHIWAWA col, which is SOUTH-WEST of the summit and is a notch in Fortress's east ridge. This variant goes to the col WEST of the summit, gained from Phelps Creek by a gully to the RIGHT of Point 5971.

THE TEST IS WHAT LIES ABOVE THE COL YOU REACH. From this one, the WEST RIDGE runs to the summit on easy Class 2 ground — a walk, essentially. From the Fortress-Chiwawa col you face slabs, gullies and talus on the south-west FACE with a loose Class 2-3 step at the top. If you have reached a col and the way on is a broad easy crest, you are on this variant. If it is a face with no obvious line, you are on the standard one.

THE APPROACH MARKER IS A NUMBERED POINT AND THAT IS ALL THERE IS: the gully is to the RIGHT of Point 5971. Nothing else about the bushwhack below it is published, which is why this is the second variant and not the first. Carry a track.

climbing_route.label: Talus/scree gullies to the ~6,300 ft bench
climbing_route.notes: Above the basin, gain the ~6,300 ft bench via talus/scree gullies or the vegetated slopes just left of them. Early-season parties will find snow gullies here — ice axe/crampons recommended — that are faster than the loose summer scree.

climbing_route.label: Southwest face slabs and gullies
climbing_route.notes: From the bench, the standard finish is a scramble up slabs and gullies on the southwest face.

climbing_route.label: Crux section gaining the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: The short section gaining the summit ridge is the route's crux — loose, exposed rock.

climbing_route.label: Summit traverse
climbing_route.notes: An easy ~100 ft rightward (west) traverse along the ridge leads to the summit.

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
bivy.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
bivy.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more
